title: Short Stuff: Two Scary True Shorties!
summary: Short Stuff episode for Halloween covering two real-life scary stories. First, the Breeziest family of Auburn, Pennsylvania, found dead animals, spices, and old newspapers packed inside their walls, which locals linked to Pennsylvania Dutch powwow protection magic and the book The Long Lost Friends by John George Hohman (1820); the hosts also recount the 1928 murder tied to John Blymyer and neighbor Nelson Reemeyer. Second, the Derek and Maria Brotus home at 657 Boulevard in Westfield, New Jersey, bought in 2014 for about $1.4 million, where an anonymous stalker calling themselves "the Watcher" sent hand-typed letters, leading to a family that never moved in, court fights, DNA testing of envelopes, a threatening letter, and a sale about five years later at a roughly $400,000 loss; the hosts mention the Netflix series The Watcher.

segments.title: Opening banter and Halloween setup
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck welcome listeners the day before Halloween and introduce two scary true stories, crediting various sources.

segments.title: Auburn family's walls full of dead animals and powwow magic
segments.summary: A family in Auburn, Pennsylvania, found dead animals, bones, spices, and old newspapers in their walls during renovation. Locals tied this to Pennsylvania Dutch powwow protection magic, which draws on the 1820 book The Long Lost Friends by John George Hohman. The hosts describe the book's protective purpose and the 1928 murder of neighbor Nelson Reemeyer by John Blymyer, who was seeking a spell book to lift a curse. The family's insurance refused to cover about $20,000 in remediation.

segments.title: Transition to second story
segments.summary: The hosts take a break and set up the second real-life horror story.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Brief break with show intro audio.

segments.title: Brotus family buys the Westfield house and first letters arrive
segments.summary: Derek and Maria Brotus buy a six-bedroom Dutch colonial at 657 Boulevard in Westfield, New Jersey, in 2014 for about $1.4 million, above asking. The house was built in 1905. The previous owners, the Woods family, had received a hand-typed letter from someone calling themselves the Watcher. The Brotuses then received their own letters, which referenced the house's history and asked for young blood.

segments.title: Escalating letters, webcams, and a family that never moves in
segments.summary: The letters grow more detailed about the Brotus children, asking which bedrooms they sleep in. Derek sets up webcams. A later letter says the house is missing them. The family never moves in, grows paranoid, and fails to sell the house. The hosts note the Netflix series The Watcher.

segments.title: Lawsuit, DNA on envelopes, and suspects
segments.summary: The Brotuses sued the Woods family, claiming they knew about the letters and did not disclose them. The Woods denied this. Testing found a woman's DNA on the envelopes and letters, and the postmarks were from about twenty miles away. Police and the prosecutor got involved. Suspects included another bidder and neighbors, and there was suspicion the Brotuses staged it.

segments.title: Threatening letter and failed subdivision
segments.summary: In 2016 the Brotuses tried to subdivide the lot and build two more houses, but the zoning board refused. They rented the house, and the renter stayed despite a later threatening letter. The letter promised revenge through accidents, illness, or a pet's death, and the hosts note its line about a plane crash.

segments.title: Sale of the house and the Netflix show
segments.summary: The Brotuses sold the house about five years after buying it at a roughly $400,000 loss. The hosts discuss the Netflix series The Watcher, which they say is off the rails, and mention actor Bobby Cannavale and Rose Byrne.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners for the extended two-part Short and wish a happy Halloween.
